common_name: Linn Perennial Ryegrass (Oregon-Bred Forage-Type Diploid Ryegrass)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in late summer to early fall, or early spring in colder zones; Linn is an old public forage-type diploid released by Oregon State University and remains a common check cultivar in Pacific Northwest pasture and seed trials.

directions: Drill or broadcast seed shallowly into a firm, fertile seedbed in late summer or early fall for pasture establishment, or in early spring where winters are severe. Linn was released by the Oregon Agricultural Experiment Station as an early forage-type perennial ryegrass, valued for rapid germination, good seedling vigor, and reliable persistence under grazing in the mild, moist conditions of the Willamette Valley and similar cool-season pasture regions. It regrows quickly after each grazing or cutting and blends well with clover in mixed pastures, though it is less winter-hardy than fescue or orchardgrass in colder inland climates. Graze or mow before seedheads fully emerge for the best forage quality, and avoid overgrazing in late summer when regrowth slows under drought stress.
sources: Oregon State University Extension Forage Information System
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet -- Perennial Ryegrass
Oregon State University Seed Certification Service

common_name: TAM 90 Annual Ryegrass (Texas A&M-Bred Cold-Tolerant Italian Ryegrass)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early fall for winter grazing and overseeding dormant pastures; TAM 90 was bred at Texas A&M for improved cold tolerance and disease resistance over older common annual ryegrass seed.

directions: Broadcast or drill into a prepared or no-till seedbed in early fall, or overseed directly onto dormant bermudagrass or bahiagrass sod for winter grazing. TAM 90 was developed by the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station specifically for greater winter hardiness and crown rust resistance than older common Gulf-type annual ryegrass, giving it better cold survival further north and a longer productive grazing season. It establishes a dense, fibrous root mass that scavenges residual soil nitrogen and controls erosion on bare winter ground, and it responds well to nitrogen topdressing for repeated grazing or hay cuttings. Terminate by grazing hard, mowing, or herbicide before seed set in spring to keep it from persisting as a volunteer in the following summer crop.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension
Oregon State University Seed Certification Service
SARE Cover Crop Database

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early fall or early spring into a firm, fertile seedbed; Potomac is a long-standing public orchardgrass cultivar released for the mid-Atlantic and upper South, still used as a reference variety in modern forage trials.

directions: Drill seed 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun to partial shade in early fall, or early spring where fall establishment is impractical. Potomac was released decades ago as an early-maturing, leafy orchardgrass selected for strong yield and persistence under hay and pasture management in the mid-Atlantic and transition-zone states, and it remains one of the most widely referenced check cultivars in university orchardgrass variety trials. It greens up early in spring and regrows vigorously after cutting or grazing, making it well suited to a three- or four-cut hay schedule when paired with adequate nitrogen or a companion legume. Mow or graze before heading for the best forage quality, since orchardgrass quality drops quickly once seedheads emerge.
sources: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension -- Orchardgrass Management
Virginia Cooperative Extension Forage Variety Testing
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet -- Orchardgrass

common_name: Climax Timothy (Classic Late-Maturing Hay and Pasture Timothy)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into a firm, well-prepared seedbed in late summer or early fall, or early spring in the coldest zones; Climax is an old Canadian-bred, late-maturing timothy still used as a check cultivar in forage variety trials.

directions: Broadcast or drill seed shallowly into a firm seedbed in late summer through early fall, or early spring in the coldest zones, since timothy establishes slowly and needs consistent moisture as a seedling. Climax was bred in Canada as a late-maturing timothy selected for high hay yield and good winter survival, and it has remained a standard reference cultivar in cool-region forage variety trials for decades thanks to its predictable performance. Its later heading date than common timothy gives a wider harvest window and often pairs well with red clover or alfalfa in a mixed hay stand, since the legume tends to mature at a similar pace. Cut or graze at early head emergence for the best balance of yield and forage quality, and allow adequate regrowth time before a second cutting.
sources: Cornell University Forage Variety Trials
University of Wisconsin Extension Forage Grasses
USDA NRCS Plant Guide -- Phleum pratense

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into a firm, well-prepared seedbed in late summer or early fall, or early spring in the coldest zones; Itasca is an early-maturing timothy released by the University of Minnesota for the northern hay belt.

directions: Broadcast or drill seed shallowly into a firm, moist seedbed in late summer through early fall, or early spring in the far North, since timothy seedlings are small and slow to establish. Itasca was developed at the University of Minnesota as an earlier-heading alternative to common timothy, reaching first-cut readiness several days ahead of standard varieties, which helps growers in short northern hay seasons fit in a timely first cutting and stronger regrowth before fall dormancy. It shares timothy's excellent palatability and curing quality for horse and dairy hay, and its shallow, fibrous root system also works as a short-term cover between vegetable rotations in cold climates. Cut at early head emergence for peak forage quality, and avoid close, frequent cutting since timothy is slower to recover than orchardgrass or ryegrass.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension Forage Production
USDA NRCS Plant Guide -- Phleum pratense
North Dakota State University Extension Forage Guide

common_name: Kentucky 31 Tall Fescue (Classic Toxic-Endophyte Forage Tall Fescue)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early fall 6-8 weeks before the first hard frost, or in early spring, into a firm, fertile seedbed; Kentucky 31 was released by the University of Kentucky in 1943 and remains the most widely planted tall fescue in the transition zone and upper South.

directions: Drill seed 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun to light shade in early fall, or early spring where fall planting is not practical. Kentucky 31 was selected from a farm pasture in Menifee County, Kentucky and released by the University of Kentucky in 1943; it became the foundation of tall fescue pasture and hay acreage across the transition zone thanks to exceptional persistence, drought tolerance, and grazing tolerance on a wide range of soils. Almost all Kentucky 31 seed carries a naturally occurring fungal endophyte that boosts the plant's stress tolerance but also produces ergot alkaloids responsible for fescue toxicosis in cattle and horses; grazing management, dilution with legumes, or switching to a novel-endophyte cultivar can reduce these effects. It forms a dense, deep-rooted sod valuable for erosion control on waterways and slopes even where livestock toxicity is not a concern.
sources: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension -- Tall Fescue Management
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet -- Tall Fescue
Alliance for Grassland Renewal

common_name: Jesup MaxQ Tall Fescue (Novel-Endophyte Cattle-Safe Forage Tall Fescue)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early fall 6-8 weeks before the first hard frost into a firm, fertile seedbed; Jesup MaxQ pairs the persistent Jesup tall fescue variety with a non-toxic novel endophyte, avoiding the fescue toxicosis caused by common Kentucky 31.

directions: Drill seed 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun to light shade in early fall, allowing full establishment before winter. Jesup MaxQ combines the University of Georgia's Jesup tall fescue, selected for persistence and yield comparable to Kentucky 31, with a novel, non-ergot-alkaloid-producing endophyte strain that still confers the plant's characteristic drought and stress tolerance without causing fescue toxicosis in grazing cattle and horses. Because the beneficial endophyte lives only in the seed and declines in storage, use fresh, properly stored seed and avoid holding it over multiple seasons before planting. It fits the same hay, pasture, and erosion-control roles as common tall fescue but is the preferred choice wherever livestock health and weight gain on fescue pasture are a priority.
sources: University of Georgia Extension -- Novel Endophyte Tall Fescue
Alliance for Grassland Renewal
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet -- Tall Fescue
